research_dossier.core_conflict: Humanity placed an eternal cultural time capsule on a trajectory that will wander the Milky Way for billions of years.

verified_claims.claim_text: Voyager 1 crossed into interstellar space in August 2012.
Electroplated with uranium-238 to allow future finders to calculate the launch date.

chronology.event: Voyager twin probes launched from Cape Canaveral.

hook_candidates.text: In 2012, an intact ship sailed alone with dinner still warm on the table.
Seventy-two seconds of signal changed how astronomers scanned the sky forever.
The radar alarm tripped at midnight, pointing toward an empty patch of ocean.
The deepest vault on Earth held fifty records, but zero visitors were allowed inside.
A three-man crew vanished from an island lighthouse without leaving a single trace.
Deep below the Mediterranean floor lies an intact temple no diver was meant to see.
Astronomers logged the exact frequency, yet forty-nine years later the source remains completely silent.
Over twenty miles of ancient stone sat buried beneath coastal sand for a millennium.

beats.text: In 1977, NASA launched two phonograph records designed to outlast human civilization.
Mounted to the hulls of Voyager One and Two, the golden discs are made of gold-plated copper.
A committee chaired by Carl Sagan encoded one hundred and fifteen images showing landscapes, cities, and engineering.
Audio tracks contain greetings in fifty-five languages, natural thunder, ocean storms, and classical music.
Etched on the cover is a pulsar map marking the exact coordinates of our Sun using cosmic beacons.
Scientists even added a sample of ultra-pure uranium-238 so alien finders can calculate the launch date.
Both spacecraft have crossed into interstellar space, drifting safely through the vacuum where cosmic erosion takes billions of years.
Billions of years into the future, stars will illuminate those two phonograph records.
